1c7cf4c637: The guide lists two things: "SDKs wrapping REST" and "websockets". In practice the questions test four things. Do you know what an SDK call puts on the wire? What the SDK does for you, and what it cannot? How a streamed response is framed and parsed? And which transport (request/response, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets, polling) fits a given job? Connection reuse and timeouts come along too, because they are where raw HTTP integrations break in production.
329bf2bb9d:
Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 owns request and response fields, stop reasons, the HTTP status table and rate-limit headers. Chapter 06 owns the meaning of each stream event and how to accumulate them into a message. Chapter 12 owns retry policy design and circuit breakers. Chapter 22 owns MCP transports.

This chapter is the transport underneath all of them. It covers what an SDK call becomes on the wire, how a stream is framed and parsed, and which transport fits which job. It also covers how pools, timeouts and the network between you and the API decide whether a correct integration works in production.
9e1727ca5d:
Every Claude SDK is a typed HTTP client over one JSON-over-HTTPS API. It adds the auth and version headers, serialisation into typed objects, a default timeout and a small number of automatic retries, typed exceptions, pagination iterators, and helpers that turn a Server-Sent Events stream back into a message. But the request and response are the same bytes you could send with curl.

Streaming uses SSE (one long HTTP response, server to client only), batch work uses polling, and WebSockets belong to your own application tier when you need two-way traffic. So choosing a transport, reusing connections and setting timeouts per layer are design decisions you make, not things the SDK makes for you.
66ef59ebdd: At 6.1% this objective is worth three or four items. They tend to be scenario stems: "the team calls the API with a hand-written HTTP client and sees X", "the stream breaks behind the corporate proxy", "which transport should the dashboard use". The wrong options usually confuse layers. They add retries to fix a parser bug, say, or propose WebSockets to the Anthropic API.
263cbb75b9: Start from the bottom. The Messages API is a REST-style endpoint: POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages with a JSON body. The server holds no conversation state between calls (chapter 05), so each request is self-contained. The response is either one JSON document or, when you set "stream": true, a text/event-stream body. Everything above that is client-side code that you could, in principle, write yourself.
4616906832:
The SDK sits on an HTTP library. In the current Python SDK that library is httpx2. Older releases used httpx; check which one your installed version imports, because passing a client from the wrong package raises a TypeError. The Java SDK's default client is built on OkHttp (AnthropicOkHttpClient).

Under the HTTP library is a connection pool of TCP connections wrapped in TLS, possibly going through your corporate proxy. Each layer has its own failure modes and its own timeouts. That's why "the SDK has a timeout" is never the whole answer.
0a22d3deee: For a Spring architect, the closest analogy is a generated OpenAPI client on top of WebClient or RestTemplate. The generated layer gives you types and convenience. The HTTP layer gives you pooling and timeouts. The contract is the HTTP API. When a new API field ships before the SDK supports it, or a proxy rewrites your traffic, you debug at the HTTP layer.
0e0dc658df:
The fastest way to stop treating the SDK as magic is to follow one call all the way down and back up. Take the line every tutorial starts with, client.messages.create(model="claude-haiku-5-5", max_tokens=200, messages=[...]). What happens between pressing Enter and getting a Message object?

There are eleven distinct steps. Each one can fail in its own way, and each one has its own timer. The exam's transport questions are almost always about one of them being misunderstood.
925b6593a4:
Step 1, argument handling. The SDK method is a thin generated function. It collects your keyword arguments into a request-options structure: method POST, path /v1/messages, the JSON body, and per-call overrides such as timeout, extra_headers or extra_body. Type hints and IDE checks help you here. But the Python SDK does not run a full schema validation of the body before sending. An unknown model id or an invalid max_tokens is caught by the server and comes back as a 400.

One exception is checked locally: the long-request guard from section 06. It can raise ValueError before any network I/O, when a non-streaming call is expected to run longer than about ten minutes.
07b2105f35:
Step 2, header assembly. The client merges its default headers with anything you passed per call. The defaults are the x-api-key from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, anthropic-version: 2023-06-01, content-type, accept, a user-agent naming the SDK and version, and the x-stainless-* diagnostics. Companion 24_sdk_call_anatomy.py prints the complete set from a real SDK build: nineteen headers on a one-line call.

Two of the diagnostics are worth noticing. x-stainless-retry-count is 0 on the first attempt, then 1, 2. x-stainless-timeout is the per-attempt timeout in seconds, 600 by default.
92cc401272:
Step 3, serialisation. The body is encoded as compact JSON, UTF-8, and the length is computed so the request carries a content-length header.

There is a hard ceiling on what you can send: 32 MB for the Messages API, per the errors documentation. It is enforced at the edge. On the direct API, the 413 request_too_large is returned by Cloudflare before the request reaches Anthropic's servers. Base64 images and PDFs are the usual way people hit it. Base64 inflates binary by a third, so a 25 MB PDF is a 33 MB request. The Files API (chapter 06) exists to move large inputs out of the request body.
ffbcecd206: Step 4, connection acquisition. The HTTP library asks its pool for an idle connection to api.anthropic.com:443. If one exists and is still healthy, it is reused, and steps 5-7 are skipped entirely. If every connection is busy and the pool is at its limit, the request waits. A pool timeout fires if it waits too long. Companion 26_pool_limits_keepalive.py shows eight of twelve requests failing with PoolTimeout when four connections are shared and the pool timeout is 100 ms.
39682361f0:
Step 5, DNS. A cold connection first resolves the host name. Results are cached by the OS, and in the JVM by the InetAddress cache (governed by the networkaddress.cache.ttl security property). That matters when an endpoint moves: a JVM that caches forever keeps dialling an old address.

Step 6, TCP. One round trip for SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. The connect timeout covers this and the next step.

Step 7, TLS. With TLS 1.3, one more round trip to agree keys and verify the server certificate against your trust store; TLS 1.2 needs two. ALPN, an extension inside this handshake, is where client and server agree on HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 for the connection.

A corporate proxy that inspects TLS replaces the server certificate with one signed by the corporate CA. That's why "certificate verify failed" in a new environment is almost always a trust-store problem, and never an API problem.
537caa5775: Step 8, request bytes. On HTTP/1.1 the request is literally text: a request line, header lines, a blank line, then the JSON body. Companion 14_raw_socket_wire.py prints the exact bytes. On HTTP/2 the same information travels as binary HEADERS and DATA frames on a numbered stream, with header names lower-cased and compressed. The semantics (method, path, headers, body) are identical. The write timeout covers sending the body.
09fd827a9f:
Step 9, waiting. The server runs the model. For a non-streaming call, nothing at all comes back until generation ends, which can take seconds or minutes. This is where the read timeout lives. It's also where middleboxes with idle timeouts can kill a connection that looks dead (section 15). For a streaming call, the response headers arrive almost immediately, followed by events and pings, so the read gap stays short.

Step 10, response. A status line, response headers including request-id and the rate-limit headers, then the body. The body is either one JSON document with a content-length, or an SSE body of unknown length (chunked transfer encoding on HTTP/1.1, DATA frames on HTTP/2).
9e670bd9b4:
Step 11, classification and parsing. The SDK looks at the status. A 2xx is parsed into a typed Message, and the request-id is attached as message._request_id.

A retryable failure (connection error, 408, 409, 429, 5xx) goes back to step 4 after a backoff, with x-stainless-retry-count incremented. This build also honours an x-should-retry: true/false response header that lets the server override the default classification (observed in the installed SDK source; check the docs before relying on it).

Anything else becomes a typed exception carrying the status, the parsed error body and the request id. The connection goes back to the pool for the next call.
be75e14337: Here is the same call as it looks to a packet capture and a log, from a client in a US-East data centre on a cold start. The timings are illustrative orders of magnitude, not measurements of Anthropic's service; your numbers depend on distance, proxies and load. What matters is the proportions. Connection setup is small next to generation but large next to nothing. And it repeats on every call if you throw the pool away.
b229375d55:
Read the trace the way an incident reviewer would. Everything before t=0.042 is client-side and network cost, and with a warm pool it disappears. The gap between 0.042 and 1.630 is the model working. On a non-streaming call it is total silence on the wire.

The request-id arrives with the response headers. So even a raw client that crashes while parsing the body can log it, if it reads headers first.

The second call shows why "first request is slow" is a normal observation that needs no tuning. "Every request is slow by 40 ms" is different: it usually means a client is being created per request.
f01a14b869:
It helps to see the SDK's features as hooks on particular steps, rather than as one bundle:

  • Authentication and versioning are step 2.
  • Types and the long-request guard are steps 1 and 11.
  • Retries are a loop from step 11 back to step 4.
  • Timeouts are timers on steps 4 (pool), 6-7 (connect), 8 (write) and 9 (read).
  • The stream helpers replace step 11's single parse with an incremental parser over step 10's body.
  • TCP keep-alive socket options act on the connection created in step 6.

Everything else, including the pool itself, belongs to the HTTP library. That's why "configure the SDK's HTTP client" is so often the right answer to transport questions.
5ef2f72017:
Line by line:

  • (1) Five attempts with no deadline means the call can take five times the timeout.
  • (2) A client per attempt throws the connection pool away. Every attempt pays DNS, TCP and TLS again, and under load the process leaks sockets in TIME_WAIT.
  • (3) timeout=None means a stuck connection hangs the calling thread forever. httpx's own default is five seconds, which is the opposite problem: far too short for a non-streaming generation.
  • (4) Without anthropic-version every call is a 400, which this loop then retries.
  • (5) Retrying 400, 401, 403 and 404 cannot succeed, and it burns rate limit.
  • (6) Ignoring retry-after on a 429 means retrying before the limiter has refilled, which earns another 429.
  • (7) A fixed one-second sleep synchronises every client that failed at the same moment, so they all retry at the same moment: the thundering herd.
  • (8) The final exception has no status, no error type and no request-id, so nobody can diagnose it.
104faef821: The fixed version is longer, but every line has a reason. Companion 18_raw_client_done_right.py runs both against a real local HTTP server. The right one completes a 529, 429 (with retry-after: 1), 200 sequence on one TCP connection. It waits the full second the server asked for, and raises a 400 after exactly one attempt. The wrong one sends a 400 four times over four connections, and never sends the version header.
4d88fc01b8:
Two details deserve a second look.

The deadline check happens before sleeping. If the next wait would exceed the caller's budget, give up now instead of sleeping and then failing.

And connection-level failures are retried even though there is no status, because "the request never arrived" is the most retryable failure there is. The one caveat is a ReadTimeout on a non-streaming call. That means the request did arrive and the model may have done the work, so you pay twice for that tokens-wise. It's acceptable for idempotent reads like summaries. It's also a reason to keep side effects out of the Claude call itself: tool execution happens in your code, after the response.
be9819beeb: The Java version follows the same shape with the JDK client. Note where each timeout lives. connectTimeout on the client builder covers TCP and TLS. timeout on the request is, in current JDKs, the time until the response headers arrive. It does not bound the time spent reading a streamed body (verify on your JDK version). So for a streaming call you enforce the read gap yourself, for example by checking the time since the last line inside your line handler.
441ba6640e:
Companion 25_java_retry_timeouts.py compiles and runs RetryCall.java against the scripted local server. It checks the same three properties, all on one connection: retry on 529, wait for retry-after on 429, stop immediately on 400.

In a Spring codebase you wouldn't write this loop at all. You'd use the Java SDK, or Spring Retry or Resilience4j around a RestClient, with the same retryable set (section 12 shows the WebClient version).
c0df7f3a23: Headers carry everything that is not the prompt. On the way out: who you are, which API contract you expect, and which beta features you opt into. On the way back: how to identify the request and how much quota is left. The table lists the ones that matter for the exam and for operations. Rate-limit headers are covered in chapter 05 and only named here.
74e346573c:
Two operational points come up repeatedly.

First, the anthropic-version header is not the model version and not the SDK version. The model is chosen per request in the body. The SDK version is whatever you installed. The API version is the wire contract, and the SDK sets it for you. A raw integration that forgets the header gets a 400. That's a classic "works with the SDK, fails with our HTTP client" stem.

Second, the request-id is your only join key between your logs and Anthropic's. If your raw client discards response headers, you lose it.
dd45035d63:
A few more headers are generic HTTP but explain real incidents.

content-length on a request tells the server where the body ends. A gateway that rewrites the body (for example to inject metadata) without fixing the length produces truncated JSON, and a 400 that looks like your bug.

On a streamed response there is no length, because the server doesn't know it in advance. HTTP/1.1 uses transfer-encoding: chunked: each chunk is prefixed with its size in hex, and a zero-length chunk ends the body. HTTP/2 simply sends DATA frames until one carries the END_STREAM flag. Your HTTP library removes this framing before you see the bytes, so the SSE parser never sees chunk sizes. But the chunk boundaries are one of the reasons network reads don't line up with events.

accept-encoding: gzip is sent by default by most clients. Compression is harmless for JSON responses. A proxy that compresses an event stream, though, has to buffer to compress efficiently. That's the root cause of the "nothing for 30 seconds, then everything" incident in section 12.
0348d26486:
Two SDK-specific details round this out.

The user-agent names the SDK and its version (Anthropic/Python 1.12.1 in the companion build). That's how Anthropic support, and your own egress logs, can tell SDK traffic from hand-rolled traffic.

When you need a header the SDK doesn't set, such as a correlation id for your gateway or a beta flag, pass it through. In Python that's extra_headers={...} per call or default_headers={...} on the client. Java has putAdditionalHeader on the request params and the client builder (check the docs for the exact method names in your SDK version). Don't edit the SDK to do it. The pass-through exists precisely so you never need to.
44789ed723: It is worth being precise here, because exam options often credit the SDK with things it does not do: keep conversation state, retry a broken stream, guarantee valid JSON. The list below is what the Python and Java SDKs actually do, checked against the SDK documentation and observed in the companion code.
aca6931768: Requests are built from typed parameters, and responses are parsed into typed objects (Pydantic models in Python, builder-based classes in Java). This catches misspelt parameters at development time, and gives you message.content[0].text instead of dictionary lookups. The types are generated from the API specification. So a field added to the API last week may be missing in your installed SDK until you upgrade. Python lets you pass unknown fields through extra_body; check the docs for the equivalent in other SDKs.
a03c125d9e:
The SDKs retry certain failures 2 times by default (3 attempts in total) with short exponential backoff. The retried set is connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and all 5xx (which includes 529 overloaded). Everything else in the 4xx range is raised immediately, because repeating a bad request can't help. If the response carries retry-after, the SDK waits that long instead of using its own backoff.

In the Python build used for the companion, the backoff is 0.5 seconds, doubling per attempt, capped at 8 seconds, minus up to 25% jitter. Those constants are internal and may change, so treat them as illustrative. Configure retries with max_retries on the client, or per call with client.with_options(max_retries=5). Java uses .maxRetries(4) on the builder.
dc583fc6a6:
What the SDK cannot know is your latency budget. Its retries are per call, with no total deadline. So a request with a 10-minute timeout and two retries can, in the worst case, take half an hour.

If your service has a 30-second SLA, either set a shorter timeout, or set max_retries=0 and wrap calls in one retry layer of your own with a deadline (chapter 12, companion 13_retry_wrapper.py). Never stack both: three SDK attempts inside four wrapper attempts is twelve requests against an API that is already overloaded.
667037fd44:
The default timeout is 10 minutes. In Python it is an httpx2.Timeout, so you can split it: Timeout(60.0, read=5.0, write=10.0, connect=2.0). A timeout raises APITimeoutError, a subclass of APIConnectionError, and timed-out requests are retried like connection errors.

The SDK also refuses, up front, a non-streaming request that it estimates could run longer than about 10 minutes (typically a very large max_tokens). In Python it raises ValueError before any network I/O and advises streaming. Passing stream=True or an explicit timeout disables the guard. The Java SDK documents a dynamic timeout for large maxTokens: 30 seconds to 10 minutes non-streaming, 10 minutes to 1 hour streaming.

Companion 06_timeouts.py shows the split timeout reaching the transport, the retry on timeout, and the guard.
8896e8d212:
Non-2xx responses become exceptions that subclass APIStatusError, with status_code, the parsed error body and the request_id. Python's documented mapping is 400 BadRequestError, 401 AuthenticationError, 403 PermissionDeniedError, 404 NotFoundError, 409 ConflictError, 422 UnprocessableEntityError, 429 RateLimitError, 5xx InternalServerError, and APIConnectionError when there is no response at all.

Newer builds add finer classes; the companion's build raises OverloadedError for 529. So for robust code, catch the base class and branch on status_code or e.body["error"]["type"].

Java's exceptions are unchecked: BadRequestException, UnauthorizedException, RateLimitException, InternalServerException, AnthropicIoException for network failures and SseException for errors inside a stream. Companion 07_typed_errors.py prints the class and the number of attempts for each status.
de5693004d: When you need headers on a successful call (rate-limit remaining, the request id before parsing), Python offers client.messages.with_raw_response.create(...). It returns the HTTP response with .headers, plus a .parse() method that gives you the normal typed object. Java uses client.messages().withRawResponse().create(params). with_streaming_response gives you the raw body lines inside a context manager, which is useful when you want to log the exact SSE bytes.
bf57dd0ce2:
List endpoints (batches, files, models) return a page: data, has_more, first_id, last_id. You fetch the next page with after_id=last_id. The SDK's list methods return an iterator that does this for you: for b in client.messages.batches.list(limit=20) walks every page. For manual control use has_next_page() and get_next_page(); Java calls the iterator autoPager().

A raw integration has to implement the cursor loop itself. It's a common source of "we only ever process the first 20 batches" bugs. Companion 08_pagination.py logs the three requests the iterator makes for seven items with limit=3.
c2a3f8e9ea:
With raw HTTP, a stream is a byte stream you must parse (sections 08-09). The SDK offers two levels. create(..., stream=True) returns an iterator of typed events. client.messages.stream(...) is a context manager that also accumulates. Its stream.text_stream yields text deltas, and stream.get_final_message() returns the assembled Message, as if you had made a non-streaming call. The Java equivalent is createStreaming(params) returning a StreamResponse (close it with try-with-resources), plus MessageAccumulator.

The helper is also the documented way to make very long generations safe. Stream to keep the connection active, and call get_final_message() if you don't need incremental output.
12c6a021ff:
Some of the most useful SDK behaviour is invisible, because it lives in the default HTTP client the SDK builds for you. Reading the installed Python SDK's source (the _DefaultHttpxClient class) shows four things:

  • It sets the default timeout and the connection limits (1,000 connections, 100 kept alive).
  • It turns on TCP keep-alive on every socket it opens, with keep-alive probes after 60 seconds idle, every 60 seconds, up to 5 probes, on platforms that expose those options. The errors documentation confirms the SDKs set a TCP keep-alive socket option, and recommends direct integrations do the same.
  • It follows redirects.
  • It reads proxy settings from the standard environment variables (HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY). So a container that has a proxy configured in its environment routes SDK traffic through it without code changes.
8e558fbf25:
There is a trap in that first sentence. If you construct your own client and pass a custom transport, those socket options are not applied. The SDK only sets them when it builds the transport itself (observed in the companion build's source; check your version). That's why the docs tell you to use DefaultHttpxClient (or DefaultAsyncHttpxClient) rather than a bare client when you customise proxies. It keeps the SDK defaults and changes only what you pass.

The same documentation notes that the current Python SDK sends requests with httpx2, an API-compatible fork of httpx. A client from the plain httpx package raises TypeError. And tools that patch httpx (OpenTelemetry's HTTPX instrumentation, Sentry's integration, respx, pytest-httpx) don't see SDK traffic unless you call httpx2.alias_httpx() at start-up, before anything imports httpx. If your tracing suddenly lost the Claude spans after an SDK upgrade, this is why.
9ab9ad6ac8:
For logging, the Python SDK uses the standard logging module and the ANTHROPIC_LOG environment variable (info or debug). Debug level logs each request, the retry decisions and the sleep times. It's the quickest way to answer "did the SDK retry that?" in a running system.

The Java SDK splits into three artifacts: anthropic-java-core (no OkHttp dependency), anthropic-java-client-okhttp, and anthropic-java, which bundles both. To use a completely different HTTP stack, depend on core only, implement its HttpClient interface, and construct the client implementation with it. The documentation advises trying the built-in network options (proxy, timeouts, retries) first. The Java client builder takes a java.net.Proxy directly with .proxy(...).
49bf08317d: It does not retry a stream after the 200 has arrived. A mid-stream error event or a dropped connection is raised to you, with whatever text you already consumed. Companion 12_stream_error_event.py confirms there is one HTTP request only.
1a82557711:
Raw HTTP is the right call in a short list of cases:

  • You are in a language or runtime without an SDK (a shell script, a legacy JVM 8 service, an embedded platform).
  • You must route every outbound call through an existing HTTP stack that carries corporate concerns, such as mTLS to an egress gateway, request signing, audit logging or a mandated client library. Often the better answer there is to keep the SDK and inject a configured HTTP client (http_client=DefaultHttpxClient(proxy=...) in Python, custom OkHttp settings in Java).
  • You need a new API feature before the SDK supports it. First try the SDK's pass-through for extra fields, then fall back to raw.
  • You are debugging, where curl takes your code out of the picture.
0357126a7f: Whatever you choose, a raw client must replicate the parts of the SDK's behaviour list (section 06) that matter to you: version header, retry classification with retry-after, timeouts per layer, request-id logging, pagination and SSE parsing. That list also makes a good checklist when you review someone else's hand-rolled client.
d4967a34de:
SSE is a W3C/WHATWG standard (the EventSource interface, part of the HTML specification) for a server pushing a sequence of text events over one ordinary HTTP response. The client makes a normal request. The server answers 200 with content-type: text/event-stream, then keeps writing to the body as events happen, never sending a final length.

Because it is plain HTTP, it passes through the load balancers, proxies and TLS terminators that already handle your REST traffic. That's the main reason LLM APIs chose it over WebSockets.
c532fd2374:
The format is line-oriented UTF-8 text. Each line is field: value. There are four fields:

  • event: the event name;
  • data: the payload (several data lines in one event are joined with a newline);
  • id: a resume cursor;
  • retry: the reconnection delay in milliseconds.

A line starting with a colon is a comment, often used as a keep-alive. A blank line ends an event and dispatches it. Lines may end with \n, \r\n or \r. One space after the colon is stripped.
9c3aad2ee9:
The Messages API uses a disciplined subset. Every event has exactly one event: line and one data: line, holding a JSON object whose type repeats the event name. It also sends ping events at arbitrary points. And it may add new event types within the same API version, so a client must ignore events it does not recognise.

Errors after the stream has started arrive as an error event, because the 200 status has already been sent. The meaning of each event (message_start through message_stop, deltas by content-block index) is chapter 06. Here we care about the framing.
36ae51afe5:
The standard's parsing algorithm is short enough to state completely, and every rule exists for a reason. The stream is decoded as UTF-8, and a byte-order mark at the very start is skipped. The stream is split into lines at CRLF, LF or CR, so servers on any platform work. Then, for each line:

  • if it is empty, dispatch the event being built;
  • if it starts with a colon, ignore it (a comment);
  • if it contains a colon, the part before the first colon is the field name and the part after is the value, with a single leading space removed;
  • if it contains no colon at all, the whole line is the field name and the value is empty.

Unknown field names are ignored, which is how the format stays extensible.
7cd2808f99:
On dispatch, the data lines collected so far are joined with \n. If no data line was seen, nothing is dispatched and the buffers reset. The event type defaults to message when no event: line was given.

The id field sets the stream's last-event-id, which persists across events until changed (a value containing a NUL character is ignored). The retry field, if it is all ASCII digits, sets the reconnection delay in milliseconds; otherwise it is ignored.

Finally, when the stream ends, any event not terminated by a blank line is discarded. That last rule is easy to miss, and it is the correct behaviour: a half-received event is not an event.
689a86f8bb:
Two consequences matter for integration code.

First, the JSON inside data: is opaque to SSE. The SSE layer delivers a string and your code parses it. So a JSON error on a data: line always points at your framing, not at the server.

Second, one event can legally span several data: lines. A parser that assumes "the line after event: is the data" works against the Messages API (one data line per event) and fails against a generic SSE source. Write the general parser once; it costs nothing extra.
92c8cbf7b4: Every hand-written SSE consumer has this bug at least once: assuming one network read equals one event. TCP delivers a byte stream. The server flushes when it likes, and proxies and TLS records re-chunk it. A read can end in the middle of a JSON string, in the middle of a multi-byte UTF-8 character, or between the \r and \n of a line ending. The parser must buffer bytes, split complete lines, and dispatch only on a blank line.
4445184654: Fixed: an incremental parser that keeps a byte buffer and handles all three line endings, including a \r at the end of one chunk and \n at the start of the next. It skips comments, joins multi-line data and dispatches on the blank line. It is short:
1bbc04d7ff:
In Java, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofLines() gives you a Stream<String> of complete lines as they arrive, which removes the byte-buffering step. You still track the current event and dispatch on the empty line (companion RawCall.java). In Spring WebFlux, WebClient with bodyToFlux(ServerSentEvent.class) parses SSE for you.

Companion 09_sse_parser.py feeds the parser 300 random slicings of a stream with CRLF line endings, comments and multi-line data, and checks the events are identical every time. 10_broken_sse_parser.py shows the naive parser losing six of nine events when chunks are 64 bytes.
8bc199b006:
Before the first byte of the body, a failure is an ordinary HTTP status (400, 429, 529) with a JSON error body. The SDK retries it like any other call.

After the 200, a failure is an error event, or the connection simply drops. The SDK does not retry these, because some output has already been delivered and a retry would duplicate it. Recovery is your code's job. Keep the partial text and, per the streaming docs, continue from it. On current models, send the partial response in a user message with an instruction to continue; tool-use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered. Chapter 06 covers recovery in detail.
23939f21cc: To see why the buffered parser is correct and not just lucky, trace it through the nastiest realistic case. It's a CRLF stream where one read ends in the middle of a multi-byte character, and the next ends between and . The event is event: content_block_delta data: {"text": "Café 東京"} . In UTF-8, é is two bytes (C3 A9), and each of the two CJK characters is three bytes (E6 9D B1, E4 BA AC).
c054de6fc5:
Three decisions make this work:

  • decode only complete lines (a line terminator is ASCII and can never occur inside a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, so a complete line is always decodable);
  • treat a trailing \r as "maybe incomplete";
  • dispatch only on the empty line.

Companion 19_sse_edge_cases.py runs this payload, split inside the first CJK character. It shows the naive decode failing with unexpected end of data. It also splits a CRLF event at every one of its 24 possible positions, to confirm the output never changes.

If you prefer to decode bytes as they arrive (for example, to forward partial text), use an incremental decoder. Python's codecs.getincrementaldecoder("utf-8")() and Java's CharsetDecoder both hold back incomplete sequences. bytes.decode() on an arbitrary chunk is never safe.
d49d3cebfc:
A dispatched event tells you something arrived. It doesn't tell you everything arrived. A TCP connection can close cleanly in the middle of a response: a proxy restart, a load balancer draining, a pod being evicted. From the client's point of view, a clean close looks like the end of the body.

The Messages API gives you an explicit end marker: message_stop, preceded by a message_delta carrying the stop_reason. If the body ends without them, the response is truncated, whatever your HTTP library says.
f412fb2db8:
Don't assume the SDK catches this for you. Companion 19_sse_edge_cases.py serves a stream that stops cleanly after the last text delta, without content_block_stop, message_delta or message_stop. The SDK build in the companion raises nothing. get_final_message() returns a message with the text so far and stop_reason=None.

That's reasonable behaviour for a library, since it reports what it received. But it means the check belongs in your code. Treat stop_reason is None on a streamed message as "incomplete", log it with the request id, and recover as in section 10. A raw parser should track the same thing explicitly: a boolean set on message_stop and checked when the body ends.
677987b409:
SSE was designed for feeds that live for hours: stock tickers, notifications, dashboards. Connections drop, so the standard builds reconnection into the browser's EventSource object.

When the connection closes, EventSource waits the reconnection delay. That's a browser-defined default, typically a few seconds, or whatever the server last sent in a retry: field. Then it reissues the same GET request, adding a Last-Event-ID header with the last id: it saw. A server that keeps a short history can resume from the next event. Nothing is lost and nothing is duplicated, provided the server assigns ids and honours the header.
a09746c32e:
The Messages API stream is a different kind of stream. It is the response to one POST that ran a generation. There are no id: fields, and there is no endpoint to resume a generation from an event id. Reconnecting means sending the request again, which runs a new generation: new cost, possibly different text. Two practical consequences follow.

First, don't consume the Messages API with a browser EventSource. It only issues GET requests and cannot set custom headers, so it can't send a JSON body or an API key (and the key must not be in the browser anyway). Browser code that talks to your backend's relay uses EventSource for a GET endpoint you design, or fetch with a streamed body reader for a POST endpoint.

Second, "auto-reconnect" libraries that blindly replay the request on a drop will double-bill. They may also show the user a different answer spliced onto the first.
04b3df0e73:
The recovery procedure for a dropped generation is therefore application logic, and the streaming documentation describes it (chapter 06 has the details).

Keep everything you received. Then decide whether to show it. For a chat UI, keep the partial answer visible with a "continuing" indicator; for a pipeline, discard and retry may be simpler.

If you continue, send a new request whose messages include the partial response and an instruction to continue from it. On current models the documented approach is to put the partial text in a user message with that instruction, because prefilling the assistant turn is not supported on the newest models (chapter 05). Tool-use and thinking blocks cannot be partially recovered, so if the drop happened inside one, restart that turn.

Account for the cost. The continuation re-sends the whole prompt as input tokens, which prompt caching (chapter 15) makes much cheaper if the prefix was cached.
bd07c27779: Where should the retry decision live? Not in the HTTP layer, which can't know whether 400 characters of a refund explanation are worth keeping. Not in the SDK either, which correctly refuses to replay a request after the 200. It belongs in the component that owns the user experience or the pipeline step. That's the general rule this chapter keeps returning to: the transport tells you precisely what happened, and deciding what to do about it is application logic.
a80ce929e7:
Polling is repeated ordinary requests: "is it done yet?". It is stateless, cache- and proxy-friendly, and survives any network. The price is wasted requests, and a detection lag of half the interval on average. It's the right shape when the work takes minutes or hours and nobody is waiting on each second.

The Message Batches API is built on it. You create a batch, poll its processing_status until ended, then fetch results (chapter 07). The errors documentation makes the same point for unreliable networks: polling for results does not need an uninterrupted connection.
df4c80d8e4:
Server-Sent Events is one request and a long-lived response. It is server-to-client only, text only, rides on normal HTTP and is trivial to consume. The client cannot send anything on the same stream; if it needs to, it makes a new HTTP request.

This is exactly the shape of LLM token generation: one prompt in, a long sequence of deltas out. The Messages API streams with SSE. MCP's Streamable HTTP transport also uses ordinary HTTP POSTs whose responses may be SSE streams (chapter 22).
50237546b8:
WebSockets (RFC 6455) start as an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket. After that, the TCP connection becomes a full-duplex channel of binary or text frames in both directions. That's the right shape for interactive traffic flowing both ways at once: live collaboration, a voice session sending audio while receiving audio, an agent UI where the user can interrupt or approve tool calls mid-run.

The costs are real:

  • a stateful connection pinned to one server instance (sticky sessions or a pub/sub fan-out);
  • its own heartbeat and reconnect logic;
  • proxies and firewalls that sometimes block upgrades;
  • no HTTP semantics (status codes, caching, standard retries) once the upgrade is done.
3a5a044b39: For the exam, the key fact is placement. The Messages API is request/response plus SSE. It does not offer a WebSocket interface for text generation (check the docs if a newer realtime product is in scope). WebSockets appear in your architecture, between your front end and your backend, when the user interaction is bidirectional. A common, simpler design is SSE from your backend to the browser too, with user actions sent as separate POSTs.
b468f6d072: Companion 16_polling_vs_push.py puts numbers on it. Polling every 60 seconds for a 3-hour batch costs 240 cheap requests and an average 43-second lag, which nobody notices. Polling every second for a 20-second token stream gives half a second of lag per token, which every user notices.
6769212735:
Between short polling and push sits long polling. It's worth knowing, because it's what many systems use when they can't hold streams open. The client asks "anything new?". Instead of answering "no" immediately, the server holds the request open until there is news or a timeout passes (often 20-30 seconds), then answers. The client immediately asks again.

Detection lag drops to roughly the network round trip. The request count drops to one per event or per timeout. And every exchange is still a normal, short-lived HTTP request/response that any proxy understands, provided the hold time is below the proxy's idle timeout.
c825665967:
The costs are on the server. Each waiting client holds a request: a thread in a blocking server, a cheap coroutine in an async one. And the server needs a way to wake the right waiting request when the job finishes, which usually means a pub/sub or condition variable behind the endpoint.

Companion 21_long_polling.py measures both styles against a local server, for a job that finishes after 1.6 seconds. Short polling every 250 ms makes 8 requests and detects completion up to 250 ms late (uniformly distributed, by design). Long polling with a 1-second hold makes 2 requests and detects it within tens of milliseconds.
3aa9fb0a48: For Claude systems, long polling fits the boundary between your backend and your own clients when a job is long but someone is waiting. Think of a "generate the quarterly network report" button that kicks off a batch or an agent run taking several minutes. The browser long-polls your /jobs/{id} endpoint. Your backend polls the Batches API every minute, or awaits the agent. Short polling the Batches API directly from a browser would leak the key and multiply calls. Long polling your own endpoint keeps the user's lag small and Anthropic's request count low.
cedc9dbff2:
It helps to see exactly what "upgrade" means, because it explains every operational property of WebSockets. The client sends an ordinary HTTP/1.1 GET with Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13 and a random 16-byte base64 Sec-WebSocket-Key. The server answers 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept: the base64 SHA-1 of the key concatenated with a fixed GUID from RFC 6455.

That proves the server understood the WebSocket handshake. It isn't a security feature against attackers; it stops a confused HTTP cache or server from accepting by accident. From that byte onward, the TCP connection carries WebSocket frames, not HTTP.
0b8cedb119:
A frame has a two-byte header:

  • a FIN bit (last fragment of a message);
  • a 4-bit opcode (0x1 text, 0x2 binary, 0x8 close, 0x9 ping, 0xA pong);
  • a MASK bit;
  • a 7-bit length (126 and 127 signal 16- and 64-bit extended lengths).

Every frame from client to server must be masked with a fresh 4-byte key XORed over the payload. The rule exists to stop malicious scripts from crafting bytes that confuse intermediaries. Server-to-client frames are not masked. Ping and pong are the protocol's own heartbeat: either side may send a ping, and the other must answer with a pong carrying the same payload.

Companion 23_websocket_frames.py does the whole exchange with the standard library only. It computes the RFC's sample accept value (s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=), upgrades a socket, sends masked text frames ("approve tool call 7", "interrupt"), gets a pong for a ping and closes cleanly.
152cae6265: Now the operational properties follow directly. After the 101 there are no status codes, no headers per message, no caching and no standard retry semantics. Errors, acknowledgements, authentication refresh and resumption are all your protocol. The connection is stateful and lives on one server instance, so horizontal scaling needs sticky routing or a shared message bus behind the sockets. Intermediaries must support the upgrade and must not apply HTTP idle timeouts blindly; ping frames keep the path warm. In return you get true full duplex with tiny per-message overhead, which matters when both sides talk continuously.
99f45b9461:
HTTP/2 changes the plumbing under SSE without changing the format. Many requests share one TCP connection as independent streams. So a browser's old limit of six HTTP/1.1 connections per host no longer caps how many SSE streams a page can hold. And the server can push DATA frames on one stream while the client sends a new request on another stream of the same connection. That gives SSE plus separate POSTs most of the practical benefits of a WebSocket for chat-style UIs. It's one reason the SSE-down, POST-up design is so common.

Whether a particular Anthropic endpoint negotiates HTTP/2 is decided in the TLS handshake by ALPN, and depends on your client. The Python HTTP client uses HTTP/1.1 unless HTTP/2 is enabled; check the docs and your client's settings. Nothing in your integration logic should depend on it.
29b81f0533: On the exam, an option that says "open a WebSocket to the Anthropic API to stream tokens" is wrong for the documented Messages API. An option that uses WebSockets between your own front end and backend, for a genuinely bidirectional interaction, is legitimate. When a stem describes one-way token display, prefer SSE. When it describes interruption, barge-in or live approval traffic flowing while output streams, a duplex channel in your tier is defensible. Even then, SSE plus POSTs is often the simpler correct answer.
5abef2f915: Buffering. Reverse proxies and some frameworks buffer responses to compress them or compute a length. The user sees nothing for 20 seconds, then the whole answer. Fix it in three places: disable buffering for the route (for nginx, proxy_buffering off or the X-Accel-Buffering: no response header), disable compression on text/event-stream, and flush after each event in your handler.
3d7daed019: Idle timeouts. Load balancers close connections that carry no bytes for some period (60 seconds is a common default). A long thinking phase or a slow tool can leave the stream silent long enough to trip it. Anthropic's ping events help on the upstream leg. On your downstream leg, send your own comment line (: keep-alive) every 15-30 seconds, and raise the LB idle timeout for the route.
fd3eb80035: Thread-per-request blocking. A servlet thread that holds a stream open for 90 seconds is a thread that isn't serving anything else. On Spring MVC, use SseEmitter with an async executor, or move the route to WebFlux and return a Flux<ServerSentEvent<String>>. In Python, use async handlers and the AsyncAnthropic client.
9cffbc7b2d:
The claudeClient.streamText(q) in the controller above hides the interesting part. If your Spring service uses the Java SDK, it is client.async().messages().createStreaming(params) adapted into a Flux.

Many Spring estates instead standardise on WebClient for all outbound HTTP, for shared filters, tracing, mTLS and metrics. Then the Claude call is a raw HTTP integration written reactively. Every lesson from this chapter maps onto a specific WebClient or Reactor Netty setting, which makes it a useful review checklist.
1d735688ba:
Walk through it against the chapter.

  • The ConnectionProvider is the pool. maxConnections bounds concurrency, pendingAcquireTimeout is the pool timeout, and maxIdleTime below the load balancer's idle timeout prevents the stale-connection resets described in section 13.
  • CONNECT_TIMEOUT_MILLIS is the connect timeout.
  • responseTimeout in Reactor Netty is the maximum time between network reads while receiving a response. That's exactly the read-gap semantics you want for a stream with pings, and very different from a whole-response timeout.
  • bodyToFlux(ServerSentEvent) is Spring's SSE parser, so you never write the line buffering yourself.
  • The retryWhen filter retries only classified status errors raised by onStatus, which can only happen before the 200. Errors after the stream starts arrive as error events in the flux. They must be handled downstream, not retried blindly.
  • takeUntil on message_stop gives you the completeness signal.
  • Flux.timeout is another gap timer (between delivered deltas), so the hard overall cap is the separate take(Duration). Section 14 explains why you need both.
a1e4ed6d80:
Two Reactor-specific traps.

A Flux is lazy and cold: two subscribers to streamText(q) make two API calls. That's why the controller earlier uses share().

And blocking inside a reactive chain (a JDBC write per token, say) stalls the event loop for every other stream on that thread. Offload blocking work with publishOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) or, better, batch the writes.

On Spring MVC without WebFlux, the equivalent stack is RestClient for request/response calls and SseEmitter on a dedicated executor for the downstream stream, with the Java SDK's synchronous createStreaming as the upstream.
cac7f29358: Opening an HTTPS connection costs a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake. That's several round trips, tens to hundreds of milliseconds across regions, plus CPU for the key exchange. HTTP keep-alive lets a client reuse the connection for later requests, and the HTTP library keeps a pool of idle connections per host for that purpose. The pool lives in the client object. Create a new client per request and you throw the pool away every time.
d8aadc4397:
So the rule is the same one you apply to RestTemplate, WebClient and JDBC data sources: one client per process, shared. The Java SDK documentation says it plainly: do not create more than one client in the same application.

In Python, create the Anthropic or AsyncAnthropic client at module or application start-up and inject it. Use client.with_options(...) for per-call overrides; it shares the underlying HTTP client. Close the client on shutdown (client.close() or a context manager). Otherwise connections close only when the object is garbage collected.
07e119a794: Pool size limits concurrency to one host. The Python SDK build in the companion sets 1,000 maximum connections and 100 kept alive (internal defaults; check your version). In practice your rate limits cap concurrency, not the pool. So bound in-flight requests yourself with a semaphore sized to your rate limit. Don't let a burst open hundreds of connections that will all get 429s. Async clients matter here: a thread pool of 50 can hold 50 streams, while an event loop can hold thousands of mostly idle streams.
08e680a26c:
Three pool settings matter in practice, and companion 26_pool_limits_keepalive.py demonstrates each against a real local server.

Maximum connections caps concurrent requests to one host. With max_connections=4, twelve 200-ms requests complete in three waves (about 0.7 seconds), and the server never sees more than four at once. Requests beyond the cap queue inside the client, invisible to the server.

Pool timeout is how long a queued request may wait for a free connection. Set it short (0.1 seconds in the companion) and eight of the twelve fail with PoolTimeout. So a pool timeout in production is a concurrency signal, not a network one. More work is arriving than your pool (or, more likely, your rate limit) allows. The right response is backpressure upstream, not a bigger pool.
29d3f402b8:
Keep-alive expiry is how long an idle connection stays in the pool before the client closes it. It must be shorter than the idle timeout of whatever sits on the other end of the connection: the server, a load balancer, a NAT gateway or a corporate proxy. Say the client keeps a connection idle for 90 seconds, but the load balancer forgets it after 60. The next request written onto that connection meets a reset or an immediate close.

Good HTTP libraries check whether a pooled connection has been closed before reusing it, and the SDKs retry connection errors. So this usually surfaces as occasional latency spikes and "connection reset" log lines rather than failures. In a raw client with no retries, though, it surfaces as random errors on the first request after a quiet period. That's a classic intermittent bug.

The companion shows the mechanism. With keepalive_expiry=5, two calls 0.5 seconds apart share one connection; with keepalive_expiry=0.3, they use two.
6a8aebe332:
Sizing follows from rate limits rather than from hardware. Suppose your organisation's tier allows a given number of requests per minute, and a typical call takes 4 seconds. Little's law gives the average concurrency you can actually sustain: requests per second times seconds per request. At 600 requests per minute (10 per second) and 4 seconds per call, that's 40 in flight.

A pool of 1,000 does not raise that ceiling. It only lets a burst open hundreds of connections that will all receive 429s. Bound in-flight work with a semaphore (or a bulkhead in Resilience4j) near the computed concurrency. Make the pool larger than that, so the semaphore, not the pool timeout, is the thing that queues.
2753283cee:
In Java, the SDK's OkHttp client and the JDK client both pool per client instance. Reactor Netty's ConnectionProvider exposes the same three knobs as maxConnections, pendingAcquireTimeout and maxIdleTime.

DNS caching is the one JVM-specific addition. The security property networkaddress.cache.ttl controls how long resolved addresses are reused. Long-lived pools combined with a very long TTL can keep traffic on old addresses after an endpoint's IPs change. Keep the JVM default (30 seconds when no security manager is installed) unless you have a reason, and give connections a maximum lifetime so they get recycled.
20afd4ff4d:
A single "timeout" number hides four different waits, and HTTP libraries let you set them separately:

  • Connect: time to establish TCP and TLS. Keep it short (2-5 seconds), because a host that cannot accept a connection in that time is not going to.
  • Write: time to send the request body. It matters for large image or PDF payloads.
  • Read: time to wait for the next bytes of the response. For a non-streaming call, that is the whole generation time. For a streaming call it is the gap between events, which pings keep short.
  • Pool: time to wait for a free connection from the pool. Hitting it is a symptom of too much concurrency rather than a network issue.
c80300daad:
On top of these sits the total deadline. No HTTP library enforces it for you across retries, and it's what your caller actually cares about.

Around the whole call sit the timeouts of infrastructure you don't control: corporate proxies, NAT gateways and load balancers that close idle connections. That last group is why the API documentation recommends streaming (or batches) for long requests. A non-streaming call that generates for eight minutes sends no bytes for eight minutes, and some middlebox on the path may decide the connection is dead. The SDKs also set TCP keep-alive on their sockets for the same reason, and the docs recommend that direct integrations do too.
7b6d2eac40:
A check on the Reactor row: Flux.timeout(Duration) signals an error if no item arrives within the duration after the previous one, so it is also a gap timer. In the WebClient example in section 12 it caps the gap between delivered text deltas, not the total stream time. If you need a hard overall cap, combine it with take(Duration.ofMinutes(5)) or a Mono.delay race.

Getting this distinction right is the whole skill: gap timers protect against a stuck connection; total timers protect the caller's budget, and a streaming integration needs both.
8a389d9628:
Make it concrete with the synchronous endpoint from scenario 4: an internal API with a 30-second SLA that asks Claude for a short classification. Start from the budget and subtract.

Reserve 2 seconds for your own processing and response. That leaves 28 seconds for Claude. A typical call takes 3-6 seconds, and the 99th percentile is longer under load. Allow one retry, because one retry absorbs most transient 529s and connection resets. Two attempts must then fit, so each attempt gets at most 12 seconds, with up to 4 seconds of backoff or retry-after between them. If the server asks for longer, give up and degrade. The connect timeout is 3 seconds inside that. The result:
bbf77b2a78:
Compare with the defaults: 10 minutes per attempt times 3 attempts. Nothing in the defaults is wrong for a batch-like workload. They're wrong for this endpoint, and only you know the endpoint's budget.

The same exercise for an interactive streaming chat gives a different shape: connect 5 seconds, a read gap of 60 seconds (pings arrive well within that), a time-to-first-token alarm at a few seconds for the UX, and a total cap on the stream sized to the longest answer you allow. For a nightly report the answer is "use the Batch API and do not tune timeouts at all".
590b49dd28:
In an enterprise, the path from your service to api.anthropic.com is rarely direct. A typical telecom estate has some subset of these:

  • a service mesh sidecar;
  • an internal API gateway or "AI gateway" that centralises keys, quotas and logging;
  • a corporate forward proxy that may inspect TLS;
  • a NAT gateway or firewall at the network edge;
  • on the API side, Anthropic's own edge (the errors documentation notes that Cloudflare returns 413s before requests reach the API servers).

Every one of these boxes terminates or tracks connections, and every one has timeouts and buffering behaviour of its own. Most production transport incidents with LLM APIs are caused here, not in the client and not in the API.
d2c9fa3ca8:
A forward proxy receives CONNECT api.anthropic.com:443 from the client and opens a TCP tunnel. The TLS session is still end to end, and the proxy sees only the host name and byte counts.

A TLS-inspecting proxy instead terminates TLS itself. It presents a certificate for api.anthropic.com signed by the corporate CA, and opens its own TLS session to the real API. Your client must then trust the corporate CA (Python: the verify= bundle on the HTTP client, or the SSL_CERT_FILE environment variable for the default context; JVM: the truststore). The proxy now sees request bodies and API keys, which is a security review item in its own right (chapter 20).

Inspecting proxies also tend to buffer responses for scanning, which breaks streaming exactly as nginx buffering does. If streaming works from a laptop on a home network but not from the office, an inspecting proxy is the first suspect.
eeacefc35c:
An internal gateway in front of Claude is a reasonable pattern. It gives you one place to hold the real API key, enforce per-team quotas, log prompts for audit, and route to Claude on the Anthropic API or on a cloud platform. The SDK supports it directly: point base_url (or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) at the gateway, and give each team a gateway credential instead of an Anthropic key.

The gateway then has to behave like a careful HTTP intermediary, and the review checklist is specific:

  • It must forward anthropic-version and anthropic-beta (scenario 1 is the failure when it does not).
  • It must pass request-id, retry-after and the rate-limit headers back, or clients lose their diagnostics and their backoff hints.
  • It must stream text/event-stream responses without buffering or compression, with a route timeout above the longest stream you allow.
  • It must accept bodies up to the API's own size limit if you send images and PDFs.
  • It must not retry on its own if clients already retry, or the multiplication from section 06 happens one level down, invisibly.
d94896ac62:
Managed gateways often carry fixed limits that collide with LLM traffic. A classic example is a cloud API gateway product whose default integration timeout is around 29-30 seconds for synchronous request/response integrations. That's fine for REST microservices, and fatal for a non-streaming generation that runs for 45 seconds.

The fix is not to raise max_retries. Stream through a gateway that supports streaming, lower max_tokens for that route, or make the operation asynchronous: accept the job, return 202, and deliver the result by long poll or callback. Check your gateway's documentation for its exact limits; they differ by product and change over time.
5a783d1bb4:
Stateful network devices track every TCP connection in a table, and evict entries that carry no packets for some period. The defaults vary widely. Cloud load balancers commonly default to 60 seconds, some cloud NAT gateways to a few minutes, and some corporate firewalls to anything from minutes to an hour. nginx's proxy_read_timeout defaults to 60 seconds. These are typical published defaults; check your platform's documentation for the values on your path.

When a device evicts a connection, one of two things happens to the next packet. It gets a reset, or it is silently dropped and the client waits until its own read timeout. Either way, a non-streaming generation that takes longer than the shortest idle timeout on the path never returns a response, even though Anthropic produced one.
900ea31790:
Companion 22_idle_timeout_proxy.py reproduces it at small scale. A local TCP proxy kills any connection that carries no bytes for 0.5 seconds. The upstream needs 1.2 seconds to answer. The non-streaming request fails with RemoteProtocolError (server disconnected without a response) after one proxy kill. The streaming request goes through the same proxy, but its upstream sends a ping every 0.2 seconds. It receives all seven events, and the proxy never kills it.

Scale the numbers by a hundred and you have the production incident: 60-second idle timeout, 90-second report generation, "intermittent failures on long prompts only".
59d94b5a07:
The defences stack, from most to least effective:

  1. Stream long generations, or use the Batch API, so the wire is never silent for long (the documented recommendation).
  2. Keep TCP keep-alive on. The SDKs do this by default, and raw clients must enable it themselves. Note that TCP keep-alive probes after 60 seconds idle do nothing for a device with a 30-second limit. Some proxies also count only application bytes, not TCP probes. So keep-alive helps on some paths and not on others.
  3. Raise idle timeouts on the hops you control, for the routes that carry LLM traffic.
  4. On your own downstream SSE legs, send comment lines every 15-30 seconds.
  5. Set the client pool's keep-alive expiry below the shortest idle timeout, so pooled connections are retired by the client, not killed by the network (section 13).
ea132d781c:
When a Claude integration fails in a way that smells like transport, the fastest route is to bisect the path.

Reproduce with curl from the same host and network as the failing service. If curl works, the problem is in your client configuration. If curl fails the same way, it's on the path. Then compare from a host outside the corporate network, which isolates proxies and firewalls.

Look at the error shape. A status code with a JSON body (and a request-id) means the request reached Anthropic. An HTML error page means an intermediary answered. A connection reset or "server disconnected without a response" after a round number of seconds (30, 60, 120, 350) is almost always an idle or route timeout on some hop.

Turn on the SDK's debug logging (ANTHROPIC_LOG=debug) to see attempts and waits. And always record the request-id. If one exists, Anthropic received the request and support can trace it. If none exists, the failure happened before the API.
